Then please add a column which is your overall determination if this person supports a > 2x acceleration due to Claude in their work.” @misc { metr-2026-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment , title = {Independent Assessment of AI R&D Acceleration at Anthropic in October 2026} , author = {METR} , howpublished = {\url{https://metr.org/blog/2026-11-05-anthropic-ai-rd-acceleration-assessment/}} , year = {2026} , month = {11} , } Copy Redaction summary: As part of this assessment, Anthropic had rights to redact any non-public information in this post. Per our approach to transparency , we had the right to disclose if Anthropic exercised redaction rights, and whether or not any of our findings depended significantly on redacted information. While we were able to freely share our highest-level conclusions about risk, Anthropic redacted a majority of the evidence we found most informative for these conclusions. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” 1 Some of these redactions are themselves challenging to describe clearly without revealing sensitive information we have been asked to redact. We share a table of important evidence we were and were not able to discuss given the redactions in our process section below. All redactions that were important for our conclusions are covered by our descriptions in that table or other in-line descriptions in the report below. Much of the redacted evidence we viewed had multiple plausible interpretations, and both METR and Anthropic researchers have significant uncertainty about how to synthesize the evidence into a holistic picture. This makes it hard for the public to judge this evidence themselves, reconcile it with evidence from other sources, and come to their own conclusions (i.e. this report does not achieve ‘transparency about evidence’ ). As a consequence, the public has to rely on METR’s judgment much more than would be ideal, given the weight of the questions answered here. From August 12 to October 29, 2026, METR staff performed a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D. 2 If AI systems started to significantly accelerate further AI development, this could lead to a sudden emergence of extreme and risky capabilities . Anthropic offered unprecedented access to internal data on their AI R&D process, including a variety of metrics on pretraining, reinforcement learning (RL), training compute in each domain, benchmark scores for internal models, AI speedup analyses, forecasts of a future model’s metrics, and interviews with relevant staff. In our first section, we share our subjective conclusions about risk . We now believe that: In our second section we share some of the key empirical findings from our Full Report : Some of the key findings that most informed our conclusions about risk were redacted by Anthropic. In our third section, we describe the assessment process : Finally, we describe the biggest limitations of our analysis: The remainder of the report goes into detailed discussion of each of the key components. We include appendices with supplemental material. Our conclusions on risk. Independently of this assessment, METR published an October 2026 article proposing a set of high-level questions about AI R&D acceleration we believe the public needs to understand to be able to judge loss-of-control risks from frontier AI development. In this section, we describe how the evidence we reviewed in this assessment changed our subjective conclusions on these high-level questions. Pace of capabilities progress. A significant acceleration of Anthropic’s overall rate of progress would be surprising, since diminishing returns and dependence on compute scaling mean this would likely require remarkable scaling in other inputs. 3 After reviewing the internal evidence, we still have significant uncertainty and internal disagreements on the team, but most METR staff who worked on this project now believe that, as of October 2026, Anthropic is likely improving the capabilities of their models on well-specified tasks at around twice the rate they did between March 2024 and October 2025. We would not be surprised if the current rate of growth was closer to 1.3x or 3x the historical rate. We have additional uncertainty in how this acceleration translates to broader and less well-specified tasks. The 1.9x acceleration [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] in the AECI trend since October 2025 described below significantly informed this view, but could be explained by overfitting to the benchmark distribution or otherwise be an artifact of the AECI methodology. On the other hand, we are not confident that AECI would reliably let us estimate recent R&D acceleration, since the data points are lagging acceleration in research and are somewhat sparse. Beyond the AECI evidence, we also saw redacted evidence that significantly informed our view on this question, and made us take this apparent ≈2x acceleration more seriously. It also gave us some indication that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, though we would be surprised if it was significantly higher. Attribution to AI. We looked at a variety of factors that could explain the acceleration we observed, including compute scaling, hiring, data improvements, algorithmic discoveries, and resolving other bottlenecks. As we describe below, we were able to confidently determine that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the rate of growth of training compute. Beyond that, there was not a consensus among Anthropic’s own staff and we did not find decisive evidence. Our overall subjective estimate is that: We illustrate these points below: Our more detailed estimates for the cumulative and instantaneous effects of AI on Anthropic’s rate of progress in AECI, and at various stages of the model training pipeline, were redacted. Bottlenecks to further acceleration. A key concern is that acceleration from the use of AI could start to compound, as the development of more capable models leads to further acceleration. As we describe below, we did not identify any clear bottlenecks (limited inputs that would prevent further growth) or steep diminishing returns to further scaling that would get in the way of such compounding acceleration, though our understanding evolved several times over the course of this assessment, and we have significant uncertainty. Because of this, we believe there is a significant risk that further capabilities progress could lead to even faster acceleration over the coming year. In this section, we summarize the key empirical findings from our Full Report that we can describe without revealing redacted information (see the process section for more details on what was redacted). Terminology: We describe growth as annual multiples and acceleration as a ratio of growth rates. We use “acceleration” to refer to an increase in the rate of growth, such that a 2x acceleration means that 2 years of historical progress is made in 1 year. If AECI’s historical trend was 15 points/year, then increasing to 30 points/year implies an acceleration rate of 2 (it takes 1 year to achieve 2 years’ progress at the old rate). For an exponentially growing variable, the acceleration rate is the ratio of growth rates. If a variable is growing 3x/year, then to make 2 years of progress in 1 year the growth rate must be (3 2 )x/yr = 9x/yr (and acceleration can be written as ln(9)/ln(3) = 2). Since October 2025, benchmark scores for internal models have been growing at around twice their historical rate. Benchmark scores of Anthropic’s models, as measured by AECI (Anthropic’s version of the Epoch Capabilities Index ), have accelerated 1.9x [95% confidence interval: 1.5–2.8x] since October 2025. Put another way, Anthropic appears to have made as much progress on benchmarks in the past year as they did between October 2023 and October 2025 (roughly, Claude 2.1 to Sonnet 4.5): Our estimated acceleration is greater than that reported in the Haiku 5.5 system card (1.7x) primarily because of the inclusion of data on newer unreleased models, explained further below. We investigated the robustness of these results to different choices of benchmark inclusion, model dating, model inclusion, and benchmark saturation. Robustness analyses find acceleration rates between 1.1x and 2.9x. We would be surprised if the true evolution of benchmark scores (e.g. as measured by an improved version of AECI) showed no acceleration or acceleration above 3x. See our appendix section for details. The acceleration is not driven by an acceleration in the scale of training compute. We received convincing evidence that the acceleration was not due to an acceleration in the scale of training compute. Further details on this evidence were redacted. Interviews and surveys are consistent with AI usage driving this doubling in the pace of capabilities progress. We have many lines of evidence relevant to AI’s contribution to progress in different parts of the model training pipeline, including interviews, self-reported uplift, headcount, lines of code, experiment usage, and qualitative reflections from leadership. We highlight three important unredacted sources. First, both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers in detail about the degree of overall acceleration in their area of work attributable to AI use (see details in the appendix below). Our overall impression was a quite wide range of estimates, but centered around a 2x acceleration. Some quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the appendix. Second, Anthropic also shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence, as the responses reflect low-effort consideration. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, and very high levels (reaching 12x in October 2026), as shown in the chart below. Note that individual uplift/speedup estimates do not correspond to acceleration rates. Sustaining a particular growth rate in outputs like model capabilities generally requires a similarly sustained growth in inputs like labor and/or labor productivity to overcome diminishing returns. Achieving a significant acceleration in the overall rate of progress generally requires a significant acceleration of these inputs. We thus care most about whether we see a large change in the growth rate of individual uplift, not the absolute level. Our more detailed analysis of what rate of growth in individual uplift might be needed to explain our estimated acceleration rates in key areas was redacted. Third, we understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation in maturity depending on the area. We did not identify any convincing bottlenecks to continued rapid progress. We did not see evidence for significant bottlenecks in algorithmic progress, training compute, experiment compute, or data that will take effect in the next 12 months. However, our understanding of the status of different bottlenecks changed several times as we got more detailed information, so we are not confident in our current assessment. Anthropic redacted our analysis of a number of specific bottlenecks. Additional redacted evidence was sometimes hard to interpret, but supports sustained and potentially increasing acceleration. We investigated a number of internal metrics and methodologies for measuring acceleration in key areas of the model training pipeline. This included evidence of progress on benchmarks and metrics of algorithmic efficiency and overall model strength in pretraining and RL, as well as improvements to compute utilization, inference efficiency and data efficiency. These investigations included attempts to understand: This internal evidence provided support for there being significant acceleration in Anthropic’s model training pipeline. Some of this evidence indicated that acceleration could be above 2x and increasing over time, but there are significant uncertainties about how to interpret it. METR staff assessed how much AI is speeding up AI R&D at Anthropic. METR staff 4 (2.5 full-time equivalents) piloted a high-access evaluation at Anthropic to assess the degree to which AI is accelerating AI R&D, and how quickly extreme and risky capabilities may emerge in the near future. Anthropic lists AI R&D acceleration as a key risk indicator in its Responsible Scaling Policy (RSP). In this assessment, we do not pay special attention to the thresholds set in the RSP. Instead, we try to develop a holistic picture of AI-driven acceleration of AI R&D. This engagement started in mid-August, and is distinct from the assessment announced on October 15 by Anthropic. Details of the engagement. The METR staff worked over eleven weeks to independently assess how much AI is accelerating AI R&D at Anthropic. Our assessment focused on three broad questions: We were additionally scoped to review the AI R&D section of Anthropic’s August 2026 Risk Report, which we are publishing separately . As we describe below, the initial contracted assessment was scoped to include a verification of what percent of compute was allocated to capabilities vs. safety. METR had the ability to request access to any information we believed relevant to understanding AI R&D acceleration, and Anthropic could unilaterally approve or reject our requests. In practice, we often negotiated with Anthropic staff and compromised towards data that was informative, not extremely sensitive, and easy to share. We give more details on what Anthropic shared as well as what it declined to share below, noting that broadly the access provided surpassed our expectations. For this engagement, we did not request or receive access to sample from non-public models. Note that neither METR nor Anthropic intended for this project to involve full “employee-like” access, meaning unmediated access to data, documents, or models. In particular, this project is not the one described in Anthropic’s October 15 update on independent evaluators . Anthropic had unilateral redaction rights over all non-public information in this report. We had a unilateral right to disclose: For security reasons, we worked on Anthropic devices for the duration of this assessment. Anthropic provided free tokens for this assessment, which we primarily used for AI-assisted data analysis and visualization. Per our standard approach, we did not take payment from Anthropic. This exercise followed METR’s policies for engaging with AI companies . We provide a conflict of interest (COI) disclosure and excerpted contract language in the process transparency disclosures appendix plus the AEF-1 checklist . Details of Anthropic’s redactions. Our ~100-page Full Report attempts to answer the key questions we recently described as crucial to answer in future AI R&D assessments in detail. We summarize the evidence sources we were given, and which we were able to include in this public report, in the table below. Table of shared and redacted evidence sources Anthropic’s redactions also meant that we could not communicate: They also made some other more minor redactions throughout, which we attempt to describe in each section of this report. Anthropic described the redactions as “aimed at removing confidential information that could accelerate other AI developers.” Key dates. METR received a significant amount of private data from Anthropic. METR made extensive requests for information on every part of the AI R&D pipeline, and Anthropic shared more information than was initially scoped for this project, surpassing our expectations. Information was typically shared within a few days of requesting it. A detailed description of the data we had access to was redacted. A summarized version is as follows: In a small number of cases, Anthropic did not provide relevant information when they deemed it too sensitive. Anthropic also offered extensive staff time and expertise to this project. We believe the two staff we worked most closely with are the two highest-context researchers on AI R&D acceleration measurement at Anthropic. Both of these staff met with us frequently for live discussion, and spent substantial time collecting data, doing analysis, and providing feedback. Anthropic canceled a compute allocation component of this assessment. The contracted scope of this project originally included a verification of Anthropic’s compute allocation, especially the allocation between capabilities and safety . However, Anthropic changed the scope of this project midway to exclude compute verification and instead just focus on AI R&D acceleration. This component was canceled before METR came to any substantive conclusions on compute usage at Anthropic. Anthropic stated this was due to wanting to keep the engagement focused on risk assessment for the time being, and that it would revisit compute allocation verification later on. We report our best guesses at ways in which we could be misinterpreting the evidence. We discuss the main ways we could be making mistakes in our interpretation of the evidence. We highlight: Limited access may have led us to miss important context or data. Despite the access provided to METR, it is clear that staff-level access would enable a significantly deeper assessment. Our pipeline of information was relatively narrow, and a small number of our requests for data were denied. Being able to read documents on demand, observe internal discussion and debate, and have frequent and diverse conversations would have allowed for a richer view. While we believe we had access to the bulk of relevant information, it is possible we missed important information because we did not know it existed or could not look for it ourselves. Over the course of our exercise, we substantially changed our interpretation of key data as more context was shared with us, in some cases leading to multiple reversals on critical questions. We believe fuller access would have dramatically sped up that process of proper interpretation, and we think there likely remain points which we may have misinterpreted due to insufficient context. None of this section was redacted, but note that some of the methodological discussion may only apply to the Full Report. We include data from Anthropic internal-only models. This includes the following models (these are the codenames shared with us; we understand they have different internal codenames): METR’s Full Report includes a forecast for a future model, but this was redacted. We use piecewise linear fits to detect acceleration. We typically estimate time trends by an ordinary least squares fit with a single estimated breakpoint; we then report acceleration as the ratio of the two estimated linear trends. We adopt the best-fitting breakpoint on standard AECI data as our default breakpoint on other graphs, to create a consistent breakpoint throughout this report. However, in some places we consider deviations from this, and test estimated acceleration as per the best fit on each graph. We organize our analysis around 3 growth rates: the historical growth rate, the current growth rate and the counterfactual growth rate. We want to assess the degree to which AI automation is speeding up AI progress. For any measure of progress (e.g. model capabilities as measured by AECI), we can estimate three numbers: The first two are observable quantities. The counterfactual growth rate we can only guess at. The following plot illustrates these measures on illustrative data: It is important to distinguish between instantaneous acceleration due to AI, as we have defined it, and cumulative acceleration due to AI, i.e. what fraction of overall progress since some point in time (e.g. October 2025) can be attributed to AI. Some interviews and documents are implicitly or explicitly discussing cumulative acceleration, though we generally expect cumulative acceleration to be lower than instantaneous acceleration, due to non-AI acceleratory factors in 2025, and due to the growing influence of AI over time. In the Full Report, we organize indirect evidence with a simple accounting framework. We want to understand if there has been an acceleration in overall capabilities due to AI R&D. To reach our subjective conclusions, we organized our evidence using the following accounting framework, but all relevant usage of it was redacted. Arrows into a box indicate that box is a function of the preceding boxes, so for example, pretraining strength is a function of algorithms, data quality, and training compute. We use the term RL to include all contributions not included in pretraining. This framework lets us start at the right (capabilities) and determine whether there has been an acceleration. Then we can go back one level to see if there has been an acceleration in pretraining or RL, and then go back one further level to see what inputs are causing that acceleration. This allows us to get a deeper understanding of what is happening to the inputs. In the Full Report, analyses were all documented in an accompanying notebook and dashboard. For reproducibility we maintained a notebook and dashboard with all results in the Full Report. Where feasible we included references to the notebook or dashboard, and most charts had a “stamp” which identified their provenance. AECI appendix overview. We expand on the main AECI analysis in a few ways. Redactions in this section. This section was very minimally redacted by Anthropic. The only information redacted was: Methodological details on AECI estimation. We use Epoch’s public code to estimate AECI values for each model. We generate 95% confidence intervals via bootstrap by drawing benchmark scores with replacement, stratified by model. Our underlying data includes the AECI scores of many snapshots per model. These snapshots differ in both dates and AECI scores. For publicly released models, we include the snapshot that was publicly released and the date that snapshot was available for use by most Anthropic employees. For example, if a model has two snapshots: one available to Anthropic employees on November 10 and one available to Anthropic employees on November 20, and the second snapshot was released publicly on December 1, then our procedure would assign November 20 as the release date. We think there are many reasonable alternative dating procedures (e.g. at first snapshot release instead of last snapshot), which are shown below in one of the robustness exercises. For models that are never released, we include snapshots that received substantial internal usage and the date most Anthropic employees could use them. We use the date at which the model could be used by most Anthropic employees instead of public release dates; this allows us to make apples-to-apples comparisons with unreleased models. These in general show slightly higher degrees of acceleration as Anthropic is holding onto more recent models for slightly longer before their public release. When we fit trends over time we use ordinary least squares with equal weight to each snapshot on the frontier. The confidence interval in the trend estimation only accounts for uncertainty in the AECI scores for each model, and does not include sampling uncertainty over which models are included in the fit. We estimate a learned breakpoint in the trend, though we exogenously impose that there is 1 breakpoint. We estimate the breakpoint is October 7, 2025 in our main AECI specification. For our robustness checks, we maintain this October 7, 2025 breakpoint to ensure comparability. Robustness: Estimates of AECI acceleration vary 1.1x–2.9x depending on the link function. We show below that estimates of AECI acceleration are somewhat sensitive to assumptions about the distribution of task difficulty within each benchmark. In principle, we could discriminate between these assumptions based on the data, but in practice most functions fit the data about equally well. We acknowledge useful suggestions from Anthropic staff on analysis here. AECI assumes that a model’s score on a benchmark is a function of the model’s latent strength, and specifically that the function is logistic (shown below in black). This can be interpreted as an assumption on the distribution of difficulty of tasks in a benchmark, including how many tasks are broken or what fraction can be guessed. The following figure illustrates a few different link functions. The logistic function assumes a symmetric distribution with exponentially declining tails. The log-log function assumes a long tail of hard tasks; the complementary log-log function assumes a long tail of easy tasks. The following table shows the estimated acceleration depending on various assumptions of the link function. Note all these link functions are global, i.e. not benchmark-specific. The quality of fit is fairly similar across each of these link functions (except cauchit), and we do not have strong a priori reasons to prefer one. We continue to use logistic for our main results since it is the default link function used by Epoch and Anthropic. Robustness: An acceleration in AECI of around 2x appears robust to which snapshots are included. We consider various alternative choices for which models to use when estimating AECI growth: Robustness: An acceleration in AECI of around 2x appears robust to which benchmarks are included. We consider various alternative choices for which benchmarks to use when estimating AECI growth: Robustness: An acceleration in AECI of around 2x appears robust to regularization. Robustness: AECI shows less acceleration when we include non-Anthropic models. If we take our main AECI results and plot all frontier models instead of just Anthropic models, we estimate a lower degree of acceleration. Notice the historical trend is estimated mostly from non-Anthropic models, while the current trend is estimated from mostly Anthropic models. There are a couple of plausible interpretations of this data: New internal models make a permanent slope change look more plausible than a one-time jump at Mythos Preview. Prior Anthropic system cards have posited the hypothesis that there was a one-time jump in capabilities at Mythos Preview after which there was a return to the previous trend. Recent models make this hypothesis look less likely than a permanent trend change. Comparing our AECI estimates to various public estimates. The following chart compares our acceleration estimate to various public estimates of acceleration. The rows denote different methodologies for calibrating (A)ECI scores for each model, e.g. by changing benchmarks, which models are included in the score calibration, etc. The columns denote different methodologies for converting those scores into an acceleration over time, e.g. by subsetting to certain models, changing the release dates, etc. Our main takeaways are that: Model 4 achieves >50% on all of its benchmarks. The plot below shows all benchmark scores for frontier models in the AECI, scaled on a log-odds scale, implying that they should evolve linearly with a model’s latent AECI score (if the logistic assumption holds). The highlighted lines represent the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4. Notably, Model 4 scores above 50% on all these benchmarks. We can see that the distribution of benchmark difficulty was very different just 9 months ago: Opus 4.6 had many benchmarks on which it scored below 50%. This lack of benchmarks which are difficult for Model 4 makes us somewhat nervous about our ability to measure AECI now and in the future. Most of the benchmarks used for Model 4 appear reasonably linear in log-odds space. A specific concern in measuring acceleration with AECI is benchmarks with many broken tasks, or benchmarks with a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty. The logistic link function assumes exponential tails of task difficulty; if we instead had a fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty, this would mean that going from 98% to 99% requires more AECI points than going from 80% to 90% (the logistic assumes they are approximately equally difficult). A fat-tailed distribution of task difficulty could cause us to underestimate acceleration; as described above, using cauchit or log-log link functions (which model the last few tasks in a benchmark as particularly difficult) results in acceleration estimates of 2.8x and 2.9x, respectively. We perform a simple diagnostic test for task difficulty. For each of the 15 benchmarks used for Model 4 in AECI, we compared a model’s estimated AECI against the model’s log-odds score on that benchmark. If the AECI assumptions are satisfied, meaning task difficulty is logistic in a model’s latent ability, then we would expect each plot to be linear. If there are many broken tasks or a fat-tailed distribution of difficulty, then we would expect these fits to be concave (we would expect a convex fit if there are disproportionately many easy tasks). We noticed there are 3 of 15 benchmarks with notably flat or concave fits. When we re-estimate AECI for all models without those 3 suspicious benchmarks, Model 4’s score increases by 1 point, from 178.6 to 179.7. We thus think there is some weak evidence for fat tails causing understatement in acceleration, but the magnitude is not large. Tokens per benchmark may be too low. Using a low expenditure in benchmarking could bias estimates of capability growth downwards if later models show higher returns to expenditure (i.e. if early models plateau with expenditure, but later models show high returns). Anthropic shared with us data on tokens used on benchmarks in the AECI. A typical task (one attempt) used about 2.5M input and 72k output tokens across internal benchmarks, and about 10M input and 94k output on agentic coding benchmarks. For a loose comparison, Epoch AI uses roughly 0.5M input and 10k output tokens on a typical task across a few public benchmarks (GPQA, AIME, SWE-bench), and 1M input and 8k output tokens on a specific agentic coding benchmark (SWE-bench). For another loose comparison, METR uses roughly 650k output tokens for its latest long-running software benchmarks, though it is possible the token accounting is not comparable. Moreover, it would be informative to see returns-to-expenditure curves for each model, i.e. scores elicited at different levels of expenditure. Anthropic’s system cards do report expenditure curves for some benchmarks (e.g. Opus 5.5 system card ). There is some recent evidence that it is possible to use very large amounts of inference compute to solve difficult problems (e.g. Navier–Stokes ). Overall, our guess is that the AECI scores for each model could be increased by a handful of points if inference tokens were scaled further. Our rough guess is that this would have similar returns across models, so the degree of estimated acceleration would be the same, though this is not something we looked into deeply and it is possible that recent models have better token scaling properties. An acceleration in benchmark scores may fail to track acceleration in real-world impact. Ideally we want to know the real-world value, or potential impact, of each model, not its benchmark scores. If real-world impact is smoothly related to benchmark scores, then we should expect an acceleration in AECI to be associated with an equivalent acceleration in real-world effects. 5 There are a number of reasons why acceleration in AECI may fail to track acceleration in the real-world impact of model capabilities: Overall, we are confident there has been at least a modest acceleration in the growth of benchmark scores. We believe there is significant risk that acceleration in AECI may not map cleanly to acceleration in real-world impact. There is considerable evidence of AI speedup. We define AI speedup as the ratio between a staff member or team’s output with AI and without AI, noting that output can often be difficult to measure or define. We now briefly survey the overall evidence for AI speedup, concluding: Redactions in this section. Anthropic redacted evidence of speedup that was closely connected to specific parts of their model training pipeline, as well as our discussion of how the evidence in this section related to our estimates of acceleration in various parts of the model training pipeline. Moreover, a claim about inference compute usage at Anthropic was redacted because it was priced in compute terms and we did not find it informative enough to request it in API prices. They also redacted sensitive details from the quotes from researchers below. Informal self-reports of uplift have been steadily growing. Anthropic shared data on self-reported uplift due to AI from a variety of sources. The most recent data is from a series of Slack polls, where staff use reactions to vote on their estimated speedup from the most recent model at the time. We consider this to be only very loose evidence: we expect the responses come from an unrepresentative subset of staff and the responses reflect fairly low-effort consideration. Additionally, there is some evidence that self-report survey estimates of uplift can overestimate true productivity impact. Nevertheless, we observe consistent growth in these self-reports, shown in the chart below. For the most capable internal model in October 2026, average self-reported uplift was ≈12x. These self-reported estimates have grown but it is difficult to know how to extrapolate them. The plot above fits uplift against time, using both a log-linear fit and a superexponential fit. Interviews broadly support AI doubling the rate of growth. Both METR and Anthropic interviewed many researchers (see details in the following section ). We used Claude to classify the quotes according to whether they support 2x or more acceleration from AI in their area of work, relative to working without AI. We interpret the results as mildly in favor of 2x or greater acceleration: The quotes, with sensitive details redacted, are in the following section . There are signs of life for fully autonomous contributions in some parts of the pipeline. In addition to the uplift of human labor, we are also interested in autonomous AI R&D. We understand that AI is not yet able to make highly significant and fully autonomous contributions to the most important parts of the model training process. However, researchers described significant “signs of life” implying such contributions could occur soon, although with substantial variation depending on the area. Further details were redacted. This evidence came from: Anthropic and METR staff conducted interviews with a number of researchers about AI R&D acceleration in their work. Interviews vary in length and depth, but we expect researchers spent significantly more time on these than answering the surveys above. To classify interviews, we had Claude look over all our notes and take all relevant quotes and code them as supporting >2x acceleration due to AI in their area of work, ambiguous or against. Each row in the following table corresponds to a single person and all their relevant quotes. Note that each interviewee often interpreted the question in somewhat different ways, e.g. whether they are referring to cumulative or instantaneous speedup, or whether they are referring to personal or org-wide speedup. We used the following prompt: “Can you please look through all the interview tabs and all relevant interview docs outside of this google doc. [redacted context]. Can you make a table where each row is a person and then we put all their quotes together. Then please add a column which is your overall determination if this person supports a > 2x acceleration due to Claude in their work.” We believe this exercise was reasonably adversarially robust. As this is an independent assessment, it is important for us to do our due diligence and understand how hard it would have been for Anthropic to systematically mislead us, i.e., how likely it is that we could have been led to an incorrect conclusion intentionally. Adversarial robustness weakness 1: We relied on data from a few Anthropic employees. Most of our data was received through two technical staff members; however, we interviewed around 15 other Anthropic employees on a range of topics. We did not notice any discrepancies between what our primary contacts said and what our interviewees said. Given that many of these Anthropic employees were chosen by us, not Anthropic, we think this would have been challenging to pull off if we were being given purposefully misleading information. Adversarial robustness weakness 2: Most analysis relied on Claude. Claude was involved in many stages of this project, and so in principle could be distorting our perception of the data. We believe Claude was deeply involved in: We did not detect any significant discrepancies consistent with a systematic bias even when checking against human interviews. We suspect this is not a significant risk. Overall, we think it is extremely unlikely Anthropic was actively trying to mislead us. However, we believe greater access would allow us to increase the degree of adversarial robustness. COI disclosure. We applied v1.0 of our conflict of interest policy when selecting the team for this project, which was the live policy at the start of this project. At the start of the project, one participating team member was in discussions with Anthropic about a possible role. They received an offer and declined it. This team member also had equity in a competitor as an ex-employee. As such, we required that all of their work incorporated into the assessment was thoroughly checked 6 by an unconflicted team member who took personal responsibility for its accuracy.
